::: {.hero}
## Heterogeneity of treatment effect analysis for randomized trials

Two approaches to treatment effect heterogeneity — model-based estimation of
conditional average effects, and randomization-based inference for the
distribution of individual effects — in one reproducible pipeline, published with
its code.
:::

## The problem

A randomized trial reports an average treatment effect over everyone enrolled.
That average can conceal variation: the effect may differ from one patient to the
next.

"Heterogeneity of treatment effect" covers a family of questions about that
variation, and they are not the same question. How the average effect varies with
measured baseline characteristics is one. How the individual effects are
distributed across patients is another. They involve different estimands, admit
different assumptions, and need different methods.

This pipeline implements both, and keeps them separate.

## Two approaches

::: {.card-grid}

::: {.analysis-card}
### Model-based

**Parts I–III.** Bayesian Additive Regression Trees estimate the conditional
average treatment effect for each patient from their baseline covariates. A
regression tree is then fitted to those estimates, summarising the fitted surface
as a small set of covariate-defined subgroups.

Part II examines whether the result is sensitive to the BART prior and whether
other estimators — Bayesian Causal Forest, causal forest, and gradient-boosted
learners — agree with it. Part III asks whether the effect varies with a
prognostic score summarising baseline risk.

**Estimand:** $E[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid X]$, the conditional average treatment effect
given measured covariates.
:::

::: {.analysis-card}
### Randomization-based

**Part IV.** Confidence bounds on the quantiles of the individual treatment
effects, derived from the trial's randomization alone, with no outcome model.

Because each patient is observed under one arm only, the distribution of
individual effects is partially identified: the method returns confidence bounds
rather than point estimates, and those bounds are valid in finite samples under
the assignment mechanism.

**Estimand:** quantiles of $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$ across the randomized
sample.
:::

:::
